https://wcti12.com/news/local/warsaw-con.text: The Town of Warsaw has confirmed that the Town Attorney, Kennedy Lee Thompson has resigned. In a resignation letter dated July 18, Thompson said they will step down as town attorney effective July 31. The letter states that Thompson recently agreed to serve in the position through June 30, 2027, but can no longer effectively fulfill the role. Thompson also said they will refund the unearned prorated portion of any compensation paid under her contract. In the letter, Thompson cited political dysfunction, personal attacks, misinformation and the withholding of important town information as reasons for the decision to resign. Thompson also wrote that the environment has made it increasingly difficult to provide competent legal advice and protect the town's interests. Thompson said the decision is not a reflection on town employees, many members of the Board of Commissioners or the citizens of Warsaw, whom Thompson says they have been honored to serve. The town clerk stated they will fulfill the request for the resignation letter from their Town Attorney when the Town Manager comes back in office. We will update this story as we receive more information.

President Donald Trump plans to highlight his record on crime and safety during a visit to New York on Friday, pivoting to one of his strongest issues as he looks to boost Republicans in battleground races ahead of the November midterms. Trump is visiting the Nassau County Police Academy in suburban Long Island, where the White House said he will release new FBI crime statistics showing a decrease in violent crime for 2025. “President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “Unlike Defund-the-Police Democrats, President Trump will always stand with our law enforcement officers and deliver safer American neighborhoods.” Trump’s visit is aimed at boosting Republican candidates in closely contested races across his home state, but just how much his presence will help is in question as he faces lagging approval ratings and a deeply unpopular war in Iran wi

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Suzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to run View image in fullscreen Suzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to run France ‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside Angelique Chrisafis in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe and Rochefort-sur-Loire; photographs by Thomas Louapre Sat 15 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Suzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash. “There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson. View image in fullscreen Suzy Bernard: ‘We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives’ The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in western France , has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said. As a summer of record temperatures parched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live in heat-trap homes . The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died from drowning in France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down. Families enjoy local swimming pools in western France But France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds. In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles. View image in fullscreen Véronique Langlais, mayor of Hauts-d’Anjou, in the changing rooms of the Hauts-d’Anjou swimming pool “This pool is a treasure that we have to protect,” Langlais said. But any sudden need for a costly new part or major repair could force the pool’s closure owing to lack of funds. “There’s a sword of Damocles hanging over our head.” In 1969, after France’s poor swimming performance at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics , and a series of tragic drownings across the country, the government under Georges Pompidou launched a plan to build 1,000 pools in mainly rural areas to encourage swimming. Over 600 were built, but those still in use – as well as later 1980s pools – are in urgent need of costly renovation. View image in fullscreen Swimming lessons for children at the Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France View image in fullscreen The outdoor swimming pool, which opened in 1973 François Gernigon, a centre-right lawmaker for the Maine-et-Loire, has petitioned the government for a funding plan. He recently surveyed rural mayors, finding more than 75% feared their village pools risked closure in the short-term. He said the heatwaves made it essential to protect pools as “the only place of leisure to relax in rural areas”. He said village pool closures “make residents feel abandoned”. View image in fullscreen Emma-Özlen Kaya: ‘We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget’ Emma-Özlem Kaya, 45, is a printmaker whose Turkish father moved to Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe in 1972 when the local tannery recruited artisan leather-workers from Istanbul. “We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget,” she said. “So every day in summer, I’d grab my swimming bag and walk to the pool with my siblings and friends and we’d spend the afternoons there with our towels laid out.” She now attends water aerobics classes there and campaigns to protect the pool. View image in fullscreen The Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming pool Nadine Lemonnier, a local teacher who is also part of the collective, remembered childhood summers at another local village pool: “whole days spent diving for objects and having deep teenage conversations at the edge”. For her, protecting rural pools that offered children swimming lessons was crucial because her three-year-old cousin died from drowning in a private pool. Across France, there are dozens of rural village collectives mobilising to protect local pools: campaigning, volunteering to help run them and even painting and carrying out maintenance work. View image in fullscreen Guillaume, a swimming instructor, leads an aqua aerobics class at the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-Loire View image in fullscreen Chris is teaching his daughter Seren how to dive at the Louet municipal swimming pool In Rochefort-sur-Loire, a village of 2,400 people near Angers, members of the local pool support group gathered at the water’s edge. In recent years, they had decorated the village with flippers and rubber rings to convince a visiting government minister to secure funds for reopening the indoor teaching pool. They hosted a poet in residence at the pool and run theatre performances there. “It’s about making our village pool the focus of life in the community,” said Nicolas Robin, a sociologist. On 18 July 1969, at nearby Juigné-sur-Loire, 19 children drowned in the River Loire on an outing from a school holiday club – one of many tragedies that led the government to improve swimming teaching facilities. Swimming lessons remain key. There are three rivers in the area and the village is often hit by flooding in winter. View image in fullscreen The Louet River, now dry, right next to the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-Loire Photograph: Thomas Louapre/The Guardian “People need to know how to swim to protect themselves in the flooding season too,” said Guillaume Lusteau, the pool’s lifeguard and swim coach. The pool sits beside the River Louet, a branch of the Loire that is usually a paddling spot. But the summer heatwaves have left the river level too low for a dip, increasing the number of swimmers at the pool. View image in fullscreen Didier Le Gall, mayor of Rochefort-sur-Loire: ‘The pool is part of our village’s identity’ The mayor, Didier Le Gall, said that in this area, with a large proportion of organic farming, health was a priority and the pool was essential, particularly for families on low incomes. “It’s important for children learning to swim, but also for the social lives of people who don’t go away on holiday,” he said. “The pool is part of our village’s identity, and in the heatwaves it has become a crucial place to cool down. The pool’s impact on mental health and physical health is considerable.” Le Gall said the town hall wanted to keep the pool open, despite the €100,000 basic running cost. “But we need help in the long-term,” he said. View image in fullscreen Louet municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-Loire View image in fullscreen Louet Municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-Loire Bruno Cheminat, 73, a former special educational needs teacher and one-time competitive swimmer, clocks up 2,000 metres every day, and has also helped with painting and maintenance work as a volunteer. “It’s beautiful to be the first in the water in the morning,” he said. Estelle, a former flight attendant who works on the pool reception, said it boosted her mood to be in the water, looking out at trees towards the church: “It’s like swimming in a picture postcard.” Explore more on these topics France Swimming Climate crisis Extreme heat Europe Europe weather features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://hungarytoday.hu/tisza-government.text: TISZA Government Decision Puts Country’s Largest Construction Giant on Path to Bankruptcy One of the country’s largest construction companies has initiated bankruptcy proceedings; the owner himself has confirmed this decision. One of the reasons for this is a government decision regarding the office complex in Zugló (Budapest’s 14th district), Magyar Nemzet reported. Bayer Construct Zrt. has filed a petition with the court to initiate bankruptcy proceedings, as Attila Balázs, the owner originally from Transylvania, informed the employees. He explicitly cited the government’s decision regarding the Zugló city center as one of the reasons for the company’s current financial situation. The company also pointed to changes in the legal framework governing the investments currently in the planning stages, as well as unfavorable market developments, wrote Dániel Deák, senior analyst at the Institute of the 21st Century, in his Facebook post on Wednesday. Attila Balázs. Photo: MTI/Purger Tamás In this context, it is worth recalling that the Péter Magyar government announced on August 3 that it would not finalize the purchase agreement for the office complex in Zugló. According to the cabinet, the investor failed to meet the conditions agreed upon in the preliminary contract; it was not possible to lift the municipal preemptive rights encumbering the properties in question. The government is therefore preparing to reclaim the equivalent of 865 million EUR previously paid. The financial difficulties of such a large company could therefore extend far beyond Bayer Construct. Subcontractors, suppliers, and several ongoing investment projects could also be affected, even though the company emphasizes that it intends to continue operations during the insolvency proceedings and pay its partners, according to Dániel Deák, who adds that all of this is happening at a time when the construction industry is already struggling. According to the Central Statistical Office (KSH), construction output fell by 10.7% year-over-year in May, while the workday-adjusted decline in June was 5%. Construction volume fell by 5.5% in June, and building construction output was 22.1% below the previous year’s level. In other words, the government became embroiled in a serious dispute with one of the country’s largest players in the construction industry at a time when the sector actually needs stability and new contracts, concludes Dániel Deák.
